title: Infinite-time questions about complex systems are almost always undecidable

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Infinite-time questions about complex systems are almost always undecidable

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: For almost any system whose behavior seems complex, almost any non-trivial question about its behavior after infinitely many steps (e.g. whether a pattern dies out, becomes repetitive, or ever produces a given arrangement) is undecidable, and such undecidability should be widespread in nature.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: for almost any system whose behavior seems to us complex almost any non-trivial question about what the system does after an infinite number of steps will be undecidable.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Undecidability and Intractability” (from p. 753), p. 755. Scope: systems with complex behavior, including simple programs and natural systems

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-21: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.39

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Many individual infinite-time questions for universal systems have checkable undecidability proofs, so important special cases are resolvable. No existing enumeration or measure supports the near-universal prevalence claim, especially its extension to nature.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define a distribution over a specified formal system family and a set of decision problems, then prove decidability or undecidability and estimate their proportions. The nature component would additionally require validated mappings from observed systems to those formal models.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Undecidability is generally established by proof, not finite data.

Modeling natural systems as exact programs is unvalidated.

"Almost any" has no sampling measure.

operationalizability: 0.35

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Published proofs already show that some very simple universal systems have undecidable infinite-time questions, so the phenomenon is not confined to elaborate constructions. The sentence extends this to almost any complex-looking system and to nature. Examples do not discharge those quantifiers, and no observational dataset records undecidability of a natural process.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For a formally specified family, such as reachability for a universal cellular automaton, a reduction from the halting problem confirms undecidability and a decision procedure refutes it. Applying that test to a sample of complex-looking systems leaves the quantifiers almost any system and almost any question, and the clause about nature, outside the sample.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Observational catalogs do not record undecidability of natural processes.

Seems complex and almost any non-trivial question are not a formal class.

Undecidability belongs to an infinite family and is invisible in one long simulation.

fields.value:

data existence: 0.6
analysis feasibility: 0.35
operationalizability: 0.4
